newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: GOLF-SHARK TAMES TIGER IN AUSTRALIAN OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SHARK TAMES TIGER IN AUSTRALIAN OPEN.

text.p: Tiger Woods slumped to the worst round of his short professional career on Thursday to finish a massive 12 shots behind Greg Norman after the first day of their Australian Open showdown.

The 20-year-old American soared to a seven-over-par 79 at Sydney's Australian Golf Club course while Norman thrilled the home crowd with a scintillating 67 before going on to play a social round on another course with visiting U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Woods, winner of two tournaments since turning professional two months ago, is one of the longest hitters in the game and consistently drives longer than world number one Norman.
But he struggled for accuracy around the Jack Nicklaus-designed course.
The round was Woods' worst since turning professional, his previous highest being a 78 at the Tour Championship in Oklahoma last month.
"My good shots turned out bad, and my bad shots turned out horrible," Woods said.
"I tried my heart out. I just couldn't execute the shots. I was out of rhythm."
Another round in the high 70s or 80s on Friday would see Woods miss the halfway cut after being reportedly paid over A$300,000 (US$240,000) in appearance fees.
"You've just got to deal with it and keep as low as possible so you don't blow yourself out of the tournament," Woods said.
"I am in a spot now where it's going to be difficult, but if I can shoot three scores in the 60s, who knows?"

Woods started badly, scrambling to save par at the first hole after finding a fairway bunker with his drive and then bogeying the par-three second. He went on to record another three bogeys and two double bogeys, his only birdie coming at the final hole.
In stark contrast, defending champion Norman sparkled as he fired six birdies in his first 16 holes.
"My caddie Tony (Navarro) was saying that was the best he has seen me for quite a long time," said Norman.
Klas Eriksson of Sweden was second on 68, one ahead of Australian Robert Stephens. Only 10 players broke par.
